graz.s: Graz is the second-largest city of Austria and the capital of the state of Styria, on the Mur river. It grew around a castle hill in the Middle Ages and became the capital of Styria and, from 1564 to 1619, the seat of the Habsburg archdukes of Inner Austria, who directed the…

grenzer.s: Grenzer were the soldier-settlers of the Habsburg Military Frontier, the border zone against the Ottoman Empire in Croatia, Slavonia, Hungary and later Transylvania. Many were Orthodox Serbs and Vlachs who fled Ottoman territory and received land, freedom from serfdom and…

greenville-liberia.s: Greenville is a port town on the coast of south-eastern Liberia and the capital of Sinoe County, at the mouth of the Sinoe river. It was founded in the late 1830s as the first town of Mississippi-in-Africa, a settlement of formerly enslaved African Americans organised by the…

great-lavra.s: The Great Lavra is the oldest and largest of the monasteries of Mount Athos in northern Greece, founded in 963 by Athanasios the Athonite with the support of the future Byzantine emperor Nikephoros II Phokas. It turned Athos from a land of hermits into a community of organised…

golconda-fort.s: Golconda Fort is a fortress on a granite hill west of Hyderabad in Telangana, India. First built as a mud fort under the Kakatiyas, it passed from the Musunuri Nayaks to the Bahmani Sultanate in the 1360s and became the capital of the Qutb Shahi sultans, who rebuilt it in stone.

gla.s: Gla is a Mycenaean fortress on a rocky outcrop that was once an island in Lake Copais in Boeotia, Greece. Built in the 13th century BCE, its walls run nearly three kilometres, enclosing far more ground than any other Mycenaean citadel.

ghardaia.s: Ghardaïa is a city in the Algerian Sahara, the largest of the five Ibadi towns of the Mzab valley and the capital of Ghardaïa Province. Founded in the 11th century, it grew around a hilltop mosque, with houses descending in rings to the walls and palm groves.

gatling-gun.s: The Gatling gun is a hand-cranked, rapid-firing gun with several rotating barrels, patented by the American inventor Richard Gatling in 1862. It was used in the later stages of the American Civil War and then in colonial wars around the world.

gilgit-agency.s: The Gilgit Agency was a British political agency in the far north of the Indian empire, set up in 1877 and permanently from 1889, to watch the passes towards Russian Central Asia. It supervised the states of Hunza and Nagar and the surrounding valleys under the suzerainty of…

gondwana-india.s: Gondwana is the historical name of the hilly, forested region of central India inhabited largely by the Gond people, covering parts of modern Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Chhattisgarh and Odisha. Between the 16th and 18th centuries Gond kingdoms such as Garha-Mandla, Deogarh…

geluofeng.s: Geluofeng was king of Nanzhao, in present-day Yunnan, from 748 to 779. After clashes with Tang officials he broke with the Tang dynasty in 750, allied with the Tibetan Empire and destroyed Tang armies sent against him in 751 and 754.

great-sun.s: The Great Sun was the title of the paramount ruler of the Natchez people of the lower Mississippi valley. Regarded as descended from the sun, he lived on a mound facing the temple where a sacred fire was kept, and French observers described the elaborate ceremonies of his court.

giardini-naxos.s: Giardini Naxos is a seaside town in the province of Messina on the east coast of Sicily, Italy, below Taormina. It stands on the site of Naxos, founded in 734 BCE as the first Greek colony in Sicily, and an archaeological park on the Schisò headland preserves its walls,…

gestapo.s: The Gestapo was the secret state police of Nazi Germany, created in Prussia by Hermann Göring in 1933 and taken over by Heinrich Himmler, under whose SS it extended across the Reich and occupied Europe. Operating outside judicial control, it hunted political opponents, Jews…

guna-people.s: The Guna, formerly spelled Kuna, are an indigenous people of Panama and north-western Colombia, living mainly on the San Blas islands and the Caribbean coast of Darién. During the Scottish Darien scheme of 1698–1700 they were friendly to the colonists, who hoped for their help…

gaspe-peninsula.s: The Gaspé Peninsula is a peninsula in eastern Quebec, Canada, between the estuary of the St Lawrence and the Bay of Chaleur. In 1534 Jacques Cartier landed at Gaspé Bay and raised a cross claiming the land for France.

guilford-connecticut.s: Guilford is a town on Long Island Sound in New Haven County, Connecticut, United States. It was founded in 1639 by English Puritans led by the minister Henry Whitfield and joined the New Haven Colony in 1643.

guanajuato.s: Guanajuato is a city in central Mexico, capital of the state of the same name, built in a narrow ravine. Silver was found there in the mid-16th century, and its mines, above all La Valenciana, made it one of the richest mining centres in the world in the 18th century.

gloria-dei-old-swedes-church.s: Gloria Dei (Old Swedes') Church is a church in the Southwark district of Philadelphia, built between 1697 and 1700 by the Swedish Lutheran congregation descended from the settlers of New Sweden. It is the oldest church in Pennsylvania.

gardar-greenland.s: Garðar was the seat of the Norse bishops of Greenland, in the Eastern Settlement at the site of the modern village of Igaliku in southern Greenland. The first resident bishop, Arnald, arrived around 1126, and a cathedral dedicated to St Nicholas was built there beside a large…

gustav-von-overbeck.s: Gustav von Overbeck was a German-born businessman and Austrian consul in Hong Kong who, with the British merchant Alfred Dent, obtained grants of northern Borneo from the sultans of Brunei and Sulu in 1877 and 1878. Unable to interest Austria or other powers in the territory,…

good-friday-agreement.s: The Good Friday Agreement, or Belfast Agreement, signed on 10 April 1998, was the settlement that largely ended the Troubles in Northern Ireland. Agreed by the British and Irish governments and most Northern Irish parties, it created a power-sharing Assembly and Executive and…

george-maniakes.s: George Maniakes was a Byzantine general of the 11th century. He took Edessa from its Muslim rulers in 1031 and in 1038 led an expedition, with Varangian and Norman troops, that recovered much of eastern Sicily from the Arabs.

gudfred.s: Gudfred was a king of the Danes in the early 9th century and an opponent of Charlemagne. In 808 he attacked the Obotrites, allies of the Franks, destroyed their trading port of Reric and moved its merchants to Hedeby, and he strengthened the Danevirke earthwork across southern…

gottschalk-obotrite-prince.s: Gottschalk was a prince of the Obotrites in the mid-11th century who built a large realm among the Slavs of present-day Mecklenburg and Holstein. Raised as a Christian, he worked with Archbishop Adalbert of Hamburg-Bremen to found churches and bishoprics among his people.

giza.s: Giza is a city on the west bank of the Nile opposite Cairo, now part of Greater Cairo. On its plateau stands the Giza necropolis, with the pyramids of the Fourth Dynasty kings Khufu, Khafre and Menkaure, the Great Sphinx and many tombs of officials, built in the 26th and 25th…

gulf-of-kassandra.s: The Gulf of Kassandra, known in antiquity as the Toronaic Gulf, is an arm of the northern Aegean Sea in Chalcidice, Greece, between the Kassandra and Sithonia peninsulas. Its ancient name came from Torone on Sithonia, and Olynthus stood on hills near its head.

gaspar-de-carvajal.s: Gaspar de Carvajal was a Spanish Dominican friar who accompanied Francisco de Orellana's voyage down the Amazon in 1541–1542. His chronicle of the expedition describes large, densely settled chiefdoms along the river, such as that of Machiparo, and the women warriors who gave…

gwadar.s: Gwadar is a port city on the Makran coast of Balochistan in south-western Pakistan, on a hammerhead peninsula facing the Arabian Sea. Granted by the Khan of Kalat to an Omani prince in the 1780s, it remained an Omani possession until it was sold to Pakistan in 1958.

garakontie.s: Garakontié was an Onondaga chief and orator of the Iroquois Confederacy in the 17th century. He led the faction that sought peace with New France, arranged the release of French captives and protected Jesuit missionaries in Onondaga country.

gnaeus-julius-agricola.s: Gnaeus Julius Agricola was a Roman general and governor of Britain from about 77 to 84 CE. He completed the conquest of Wales by crushing the Ordovices and taking Anglesey, then campaigned in northern Britain and defeated the Caledonians at Mons Graupius.

gosanke.s: The Gosanke, the 'three honourable houses', were the three senior branch families of the Tokugawa, founded by sons of Tokugawa Ieyasu: the Owari, Kii and Mito houses. They ranked above all other daimyo and could supply an heir if the main line of shoguns died out, as happened…

gaius-gracchus.s: Gaius Gracchus was a Roman tribune of the plebs in 123 and 122 BCE who continued the reforms of his brother Tiberius. His laws provided subsidised grain for citizens, gave the equestrians control of the extortion court and founded colonies, including Junonia on the site of…

gordian-ii.s: Gordian II was Roman emperor for about three weeks in 238, jointly with his father Gordian I. When a revolt at Thysdrus in Africa proclaimed the elderly proconsul emperor against Maximinus Thrax, the Senate recognised both.

gordian-iii.s: Gordian III was Roman emperor from 238 to 244, raised to the throne at thirteen after the deaths of his grandfather Gordian I, his uncle Gordian II and the senatorial emperors Pupienus and Balbinus. Guided by his praetorian prefect Timesitheus, he disbanded the Third Legion…

gadadhar-singha.s: Gadadhar Singha was king of the Ahom kingdom of Assam from 1681 to 1696 and founder of the Tungkhungia line of Ahom kings. Coming to power after years in which ministers made and unmade kings, he restored royal authority, expelled the Mughals from Guwahati after the Battle of…

garhgaon.s: Garhgaon was a capital of the Ahom kingdom, about 13 kilometres east of present-day Sivasagar in Assam, India. King Suklenmung moved the court there around 1540, and it remained a principal royal seat into the eighteenth century.

gaurinath-singha.s: Gaurinath Singha was king of the Ahom kingdom of Assam from 1780 to 1795, in the worst years of the Moamoria rebellion. Driven from his capital by the rebels, he fled to Guwahati and in 1792 asked the British East India Company for help; a small force under Captain Thomas…

great-mosque-of-tlemcen.s: The Great Mosque of Tlemcen is the principal mosque of Tlemcen in north-western Algeria, founded under the Almoravid ruler Yusuf ibn Tashfin and rebuilt and enlarged under his son Ali ibn Yusuf in 1136. Its ribbed dome before the mihrab, with interlacing arches inspired by the…

general-council-of-andorra.s: The General Council, or Consell General, is the parliament of Andorra. It developed from the Consell de la Terra, an assembly of parish representatives created in 1419, and from 1702 met at the Casa de la Vall in Andorra la Vella.

giosafat-barbaro.s: Giosafat Barbaro was a Venetian merchant, diplomat and traveller. After many years of trade at Tana on the Sea of Azov, he was sent in 1473 as ambassador to the Aq Qoyunlu ruler Uzun Hasan to promote an alliance against the Ottoman Empire, and stayed in Persia until after Uzun…

gulf-of-thailand.s: The Gulf of Thailand, formerly the Gulf of Siam, is an inlet of the South China Sea bordered by Thailand, Cambodia, Vietnam and Malaysia. The Chao Phraya river flows into its northern end, and its sheltered waters gave the kingdoms of Ayutthaya and Bangkok access to the trade…

geum-river.s: The Geum River is one of the major rivers of South Korea, flowing about 400 kilometres from North Jeolla through Daejeon and South Chungcheong to the Yellow Sea near Gunsan. Its valley held Ungjin (Gongju) and Sabi (Buyeo), the later capitals of Baekje.

go-heung.s: Go Heung was a scholar at the court of Baekje in the fourth century. According to the Samguk sagi, he compiled the Seogi, a history of Baekje, during the reign of King Geunchogo (346–375), the first recorded work of national history in Korea.

goi-of-baekje.s: Goi was the eighth king of Baekje, traditionally reigning from 234 to 286. The Samguk sagi credits him with organising the central government, creating a system of sixteen official ranks and regulating official dress.

gesu-daraz.s: Gesu Daraz, Sayyid Muhammad Husayni, was a Sufi saint of the Chishti order, a disciple of Nasir ud-Din Chiragh of Delhi. He left Delhi before Timur's attack of 1398 and settled at Gulbarga, the Bahmani capital, where Sultan Firuz Shah received him.

gorey.s: Gorey is a harbour village on the east coast of Jersey, in the parish of Grouville and St Martin, facing the coast of Normandy. It is overlooked by Mont Orgueil Castle, built after 1204 to defend the island against France.

geolsa-biu.s: Geolsa Biu was a chief of the Mohe people who led his followers east from the Yingzhou region of Tang China after the Khitan revolt of 696, together with the Goguryeo leader Dae Jung-sang. He refused a Tang offer of a title and was killed in battle with a pursuing Tang army.

george-westbeech.s: George Westbeech was an English hunter and trader who from the early 1870s traded across the Zambezi from Pandamatenga, in what is now Botswana. Trusted by the Lozi kings Sipopa and Lewanika, he exported ivory in exchange for guns and goods and became an influential figure at…

gaudiya-vaishnavism.s: Gaudiya Vaishnavism is a Hindu devotional movement founded in Bengal by Chaitanya Mahaprabhu (1486–1534), centred on the worship of Krishna and Radha through ecstatic chanting of their names. Its theology was set out by Chaitanya's followers, especially the brothers Rupa and…

ghiyasuddin-azam-shah.s: Ghiyasuddin Azam Shah was sultan of Bengal from about 1390 to 1411, the third ruler of the Ilyas Shahi dynasty. His reign was prosperous and peaceful.

ghiyasuddin-mahmud-shah.s: Ghiyasuddin Mahmud Shah was the last sultan of the Husain Shahi dynasty of Bengal, reigning from 1533 to 1538. He came to power by killing his nephew and faced the Afghan leader Sher Khan Sur, who defeated his army at Surajgarh in 1534 and took Gaur in 1538, despite help from…

gorgippia.s: Gorgippia was an ancient Greek city on the Black Sea coast east of the Kerch Strait, on the site of modern Anapa in Russia. It developed from an earlier port of the Sindi and was renamed after Gorgippus, a member of the ruling Spartocid family, in the fourth century BCE.

government-of-india-act-1919.s: The Government of India Act 1919 was a British law that put into effect the Montagu–Chelmsford reforms promised by the Montagu Declaration of 1917. It introduced dyarchy in the provinces of British India, transferring some departments such as education and health to ministers…

government-of-india-act-1935.s: The Government of India Act 1935 was the longest act passed by the British Parliament up to that time and the last constitution of British India. It granted autonomy to the provinces, ended dyarchy, widened the franchise and proposed an all-India federation including the…

gorgan.s: Gorgan, historically Gurgan or Jurjan, is a city and region on the south-eastern shore of the Caspian Sea in northern Iran, the ancient Hyrcania. In the early Islamic period it was a prosperous province and the base of the Ziyarid dynasty, which contested it with the Buyids…

gerard-of-cremona.s: Gerard of Cremona was an Italian scholar who worked in Toledo and translated scores of Arabic scientific and philosophical works into Latin. His translations included Ptolemy's Almagest, Avicenna's Canon of Medicine, works of Euclid, Aristotle and al-Khwarizmi, and the surgery…

gormaz-castle.s: Gormaz Castle is a fortress on a ridge above the Duero river in the province of Soria, Spain, one of the largest castles in Europe. Built by the Caliphate of Córdoba and rebuilt in the 960s under al-Hakam II, it guarded the frontier against the Christian kingdoms of the north.

greifensee.s: Greifensee is a small town and lake in the canton of Zürich, Switzerland, east of the city of Zürich. Its castle was the seat of a lordship that Zürich acquired in 1402, and it became one of the city's rural bailiwicks.

grossmunster.s: The Grossmünster is a Romanesque church in Zürich, by tradition founded on the graves of the city's patron saints Felix and Regula, with twin towers that are a landmark of the city. Built mainly between about 1100 and 1220 as a collegiate church, it became the centre of the…

george-elphinstone-1st-viscount-keith.s: George Elphinstone, later Viscount Keith, was a British admiral of the Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars. In 1795 he commanded the fleet that, with troops under James Craig, took the Cape from the Dutch, and in 1796 he captured a Dutch squadron in Saldanha Bay.

glen-grey-act.s: The Glen Grey Act was a law of the Cape Colony passed in 1894 under Prime Minister Cecil Rhodes. It introduced individual land tenure in small plots for Africans in the Glen Grey district and later other areas, with local councils, and a labour tax on men who did not work…

gobustan.s: Gobustan is a rocky upland south-west of Baku in Azerbaijan, protected as a national reserve and inscribed by UNESCO in 2007 for its thousands of rock carvings, made from the late Palaeolithic onwards. At the foot of Boyukdash mountain a Latin inscription records a detachment…

gaius-hostilius-mancinus.s: Gaius Hostilius Mancinus was a Roman consul of 137 BCE who commanded against Numantia in the Numantine War. Trapped by the Numantines, he surrendered with about 20,000 men and accepted a treaty negotiated by his quaestor Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus.

gracchurris.s: Gracchurris was a town founded in 179 BCE by the Roman governor Tiberius Sempronius Gracchus on the site of the native settlement of Ilurcis, near modern Alfaro in La Rioja, Spain. Named after its founder, it was one of the first Roman foundations in the Ebro valley and helped…

glaucus-of-chios.s: Glaucus of Chios was a Greek metalworker of the Archaic period whom Herodotus credits with inventing the welding of iron. His most famous work was an iron stand for a silver mixing bowl dedicated at Delphi by King Alyattes of Lydia, which ancient visitors still admired…

giorgio-interiano.s: Giorgio Interiano was a Genoese traveller and writer who visited Circassia in the late fifteenth century. His short account of the Circassians, published in Venice in 1502, described their society, customs, warfare and religion, and is one of the earliest European ethnographic…

god-save-the-king.s: God Save the King, or God Save the Queen when the monarch is female, is the national anthem of the United Kingdom, first published in the 1740s. It served as the national anthem of Australia and other dominions until they adopted their own; in Australia it was replaced by…

gough-whitlam.s: Gough Whitlam was the Labor prime minister of Australia from 1972 to 1975. His government ended conscription and withdrew from the Vietnam War, recognised the People's Republic of China, formally ended the White Australia policy and introduced universal health insurance and…

george-washington-williams.s: George Washington Williams was an African American Civil War veteran, minister, lawyer and historian, author of a pioneering History of the Negro Race in America. After visiting the Congo Free State in 1890 he wrote an Open Letter to Leopold II denouncing the abuses he saw,…

galbert-of-bruges.s: Galbert of Bruges was a cleric and notary in the service of the counts of Flanders. His Latin account of the murder of Count Charles the Good in 1127 and the succession crisis that followed, written almost day by day as events unfolded, is one of the most detailed contemporary…

ghent-altarpiece.s: The Ghent Altarpiece, or Adoration of the Mystic Lamb, is a large folding polyptych in St Bavo's Cathedral, Ghent, completed in 1432. An inscription credits it to Hubert van Eyck and his brother Jan van Eyck.

grote-brief.s: The Grote Brief ('Great Account') is the general account of the revenues of the counts of Flanders for the year 1187, drawn up by the count's central financial officials. It lists the income in money and kind from the comital domains across the county and is one of the…

gislebert-of-mons.s: Gislebert of Mons was a cleric and chancellor of Count Baldwin V of Hainaut. His Latin Chronicle of Hainaut, covering the county's history to 1195, gives a detailed first-hand account of the counts' politics, marriages and diplomacy, of feudal ties in the Low Countries and of…

gellone-abbey.s: Gellone Abbey is a Benedictine abbey founded in 804 by William of Gellone, count of Toulouse, in a gorge of the Hérault valley in Languedoc. William retired there as a monk and died there, and his cult, with a relic of the True Cross, made the abbey a stop on the pilgrimage…

gazi-ii-giray.s: Gazi II Giray was khan of Crimea from 1588 to 1607, with a brief interruption in 1596. He led Crimean forces in the Ottoman wars against Persia and in the Long Turkish War in Hungary, and raided Muscovy, reaching the outskirts of Moscow in 1591.

giray-dynasty.s: The Giray dynasty was the ruling house of the Crimean Khanate from its foundation around 1441 until the Russian annexation in 1783. Descended from Genghis Khan through Jochi's son Tuqa-Timur, the Girays enjoyed great prestige in the steppe and Islamic worlds; under Ottoman…

great-abatis-line.s: The Great Abatis Line was a defensive line of felled trees, earthworks and forts built by Muscovy in the sixteenth and early seventeenth centuries to protect its southern lands from Crimean Tatar raids. Running for hundreds of kilometres south of Moscow through towns such as…

gonzalo-fernandez-de-cordoba.s: Gonzalo Fernández de Córdoba, known as the Great Captain, was a Castilian general who fought in the conquest of Granada and then commanded Spanish armies in Italy. Combining pikemen, arquebusiers and fortified positions, he defeated the French at Cerignola and the Garigliano…

granada-war.s: The Granada War was the campaign of Isabella I and Ferdinand II against the Nasrid Emirate of Granada, the last Muslim state in the Iberian peninsula. Fought with large armies and siege artillery, it took the emirate's towns one by one, helped by quarrels within the Nasrid…

gustav-husak.s: Gustáv Husák was a Slovak communist who was imprisoned in the 1950s but rehabilitated in the 1960s. After the Warsaw Pact invasion he replaced Alexander Dubček as party leader in 1969 and presided over the period of normalisation, with purges and censorship.

geoffrey-bibby.s: Geoffrey Bibby was a British archaeologist who worked in Denmark at the Moesgaard Museum in Aarhus. From 1953, with P.

godfrey-iii-count-of-louvain.s: Godfrey III was count of Louvain and Brussels and titular duke of Lower Lorraine from 1142 until his death in 1190. Succeeding his father as an infant, he ended the long feud with the Berthout lords of Grimbergen in 1159 and strengthened his family's hold on the lands that…

grandes-heures-of-anne-of-brittany.n: Grandes Heures of Anne of Brittany
grandes-heures-of-anne-of-brittany.s: The Grandes Heures of Anne of Brittany is an illuminated book of hours painted by Jean Bourdichon for Anne of Brittany, queen of France, in about 1503–1508. Its full-page miniatures and its borders of more than 300 plants, painted with their French and Latin names, make it one…

guerande.s: Guérande is a walled town in the Loire-Atlantique department of western France, on the peninsula between the Loire estuary and the Vilaine. Its salt marshes have produced sea salt since the early Middle Ages, a major export of the Duchy of Brittany.

gamay.s: Gamay is a red wine grape of eastern France, the main grape of Beaujolais. In 1395 Duke Philip the Bold of Burgundy ordered it uprooted from the duchy's vineyards, calling it a 'very bad and disloyal' plant, to protect the reputation of Burgundy wines made from Pinot noir.

gaston-duke-of-orleans.s: Gaston, Duke of Orléans, was the younger brother of Louis XIII of France and for many years heir to the throne. He took part in repeated plots against Cardinal Richelieu, and in 1632 secretly married Marguerite of Lorraine, sister of Duke Charles IV, which helped provoke the…

georges-de-la-tour.s: Georges de La Tour was a painter from the Duchy of Lorraine who worked mainly at Lunéville. He is known for religious and genre scenes, many lit by a single candle, influenced by the followers of Caravaggio, and he received the title of painter in ordinary to Louis XIII.

godfrey-iii-duke-of-lower-lorraine.n: Godfrey III, Duke of Lower Lorraine
godfrey-iii-duke-of-lower-lorraine.s: Godfrey III, called the Bearded, was the son of Gothelo I and became duke of Upper Lorraine in 1044. Denied the whole of his father's inheritance by Emperor Henry III, he rebelled repeatedly and lost his duchy in 1047.

gothelo-i-duke-of-lorraine.s: Gothelo I was duke of Lower Lorraine from 1023 and of Upper Lorraine from 1033, reuniting the two duchies of Lotharingia under one ruler. A loyal vassal of Emperor Conrad II, he defended the western frontier of the Empire and defeated and killed Odo II of Blois at the Battle…

geoffrey-ii-count-of-anjou.s: Geoffrey II, called Martel, was count of Anjou from 1040, the son of Fulk Nerra. He expanded Angevin power by taking Touraine from the house of Blois in 1044 and dominating the county of Maine, which brought him into conflict with Duke William of Normandy.

gisors.s: Gisors is a town on the Epte in the Eure department of Normandy, in the Vexin. Its castle, begun under William Rufus at the end of the eleventh century, was a key fortress on the frontier between Normandy and the French kingdom and was often fought over.

grand-coutumier-de-normandie.s: The Grand coutumier de Normandie is a compilation of the customary law of Normandy, written in Latin in the mid-thirteenth century and soon translated into French. Officially revised in 1583 as the Coutume de Normandie, it remained the law of the province until the French…

giambattista-bodoni.s: Giambattista Bodoni was an Italian printer and type designer from Saluzzo who directed the ducal printing house in Parma from 1768. His elegant typefaces, with strong contrast between thick and thin strokes, defined the modern or Didone style, and his Manuale tipografico was…

giovanni-battista-aleotti.s: Giovanni Battista Aleotti was an Italian architect and engineer from Argenta who worked for the dukes of Ferrara and later for the Farnese of Parma. He designed the Teatro Farnese, built in 1618 inside the Palazzo della Pilotta in Parma, one of the earliest theatres with a…

guarino-guarini.s: Guarino Guarini was an Italian architect, mathematician and Theatine priest from Modena who worked in Turin for the dukes of Savoy from 1666. His daring designs, based on complex geometry, include the Chapel of the Holy Shroud with its cone of stacked arches, the church of San…

golden-bull-of-1222.s: The Golden Bull of 1222 was a charter issued by King Andrew II of Hungary under pressure from the lesser nobility and royal servants, who were angered by his lavish grants of royal estates. It guaranteed their freedom from taxation and arbitrary arrest, limited military…

gelderland.s: Gelderland is a province in the east of the Netherlands, with its capital at Arnhem. It descends from the medieval county and later Duchy of Guelders, which Emperor Charles V acquired in 1543.

goejanverwellesluis.s: Goejanverwellesluis is a lock and hamlet on the Hollandse IJssel near Gouda, in South Holland. On 28 June 1787 Patriot militiamen stopped Princess Wilhelmina of Prussia there as she travelled to The Hague to rally support for her husband, Stadtholder William V.

grobogan-regency.s: Grobogan is a regency in Central Java, Indonesia, east of Semarang, with its seat at Purwodadi. Under the Dutch Cultivation System it was struck by a severe famine in 1849–1850, when crop failures combined with the burdens of forced cultivation killed many thousands of people.

galdan-tseren.s: Galdan Tseren was ruler of the Dzungar Khanate from 1727 to 1745, the son and successor of Tsewang Rabtan. He fought the Qing for Mongolia, destroying a Qing army at Hoton Nor in 1731 before being defeated near Erdene Zuu in 1732, and a peace in 1739 fixed the frontier.

ge-hong.s: Ge Hong was a Chinese scholar, alchemist and Daoist writer of the Eastern Jin period from the region south of the Yangtze. His Baopuzi (The Master Who Embraces Simplicity) gathered teachings on alchemy, longevity and the pursuit of immortality, alongside essays on government…

german-palatines.s: The Palatines were German emigrants from the Electoral Palatinate and neighbouring Rhineland territories who left in large numbers in the eighteenth century, driven by war, poverty and religious pressure. About 13,000 reached London in 1709, and many were settled in the Hudson…

georgius-agricola.s: Georgius Agricola was a German physician and scholar, often called the father of mineralogy. Working as a town doctor at Joachimsthal and Chemnitz, he studied the mines of the Ore Mountains and wrote De re metallica, published in 1556, a year after his death: a systematic…

green-vault.s: The Green Vault (Grünes Gewölbe) in Dresden is the treasury museum of the Saxon electors, created by Augustus the Strong between 1723 and 1730 in rooms of Dresden Castle. It displays one of the largest collections of precious objects in Europe, including works by the court…

generalife.s: The Generalife is the summer palace and garden estate of the Nasrid emirs of Granada, on the hill beside the Alhambra. Built in the early fourteenth century, probably under Muhammad III, and redecorated under Ismail I, it is known for the Court of the Water Channel, a long…

gregory-chioniades.s: Gregory Chioniades was a Byzantine astronomer who travelled around 1295–1300 from Trebizond to Tabriz to study astronomy at the court of the Mongol Ilkhans. He translated Persian astronomical tables and texts into Greek, introducing Islamic astronomy to Byzantium.

gospel-of-john.s: The Gospel of John is the fourth of the canonical gospels of the New Testament, probably written around 90–110 CE. Its account of Jesus differs from the other three gospels, with long discourses and a high Christology that opens with the Word (Logos) made flesh.

gavril-radomir.s: Gavril Radomir (died 1015) was tsar of Bulgaria from 1014 to 1015, succeeding his father Samuel after the disaster at Kleidion. He tried to continue the resistance against the Byzantine emperor Basil II but was murdered after about a year by his cousin Ivan Vladislav, who took…

gennobaudes.s: Gennobaudes was a Frankish king of the late 3rd century who submitted to the Roman emperor Maximian around 288. After Maximian's campaigns across the Rhine, he received his kingdom back as a client of Rome, as described in a Latin panegyric.

godegisel.s: Godegisel (died 406) was king of the Hasding Vandals at the time of the great crossing of the Rhine. As the Vandals, Alans and Suebi moved west, Godegisel was killed in battle with Frankish federates of Rome, and the Vandals were saved only by the intervention of the Alans.

gaul.s: Gaul was the region of western Europe inhabited by Celtic peoples, roughly present-day France, Belgium, Luxembourg and parts of Switzerland, the Netherlands, Germany and northern Italy. Conquered by Rome in stages, culminating in Julius Caesar's campaigns of 58–50 BCE, it…

goths.s: The Goths were a Germanic people who by the 3rd century lived north of the Black Sea and the lower Danube, from where they raided the Roman Empire. They later divided into the Visigoths and Ostrogoths, who after migrations across the empire founded kingdoms in Gaul, Spain and…

gotthold-ephraim-lessing.s: Gotthold Ephraim Lessing (1729–1781) was a German dramatist, critic and philosopher of the Enlightenment. His Hamburg Dramaturgy, written for the city's short-lived National Theatre in 1767–1769, laid foundations of German dramatic criticism, and his plays Minna von Barnhelm,…

great-fire-of-hamburg.s: The Great Fire of Hamburg broke out on 5 May 1842 and burned for four days, destroying about a quarter of the old town, including the town hall and several churches. About fifty people died and some 20,000 were left homeless.

gelnhausen-privilege.s: The Gelnhausen Privilege was a charter issued by Emperor Frederick Barbarossa at Gelnhausen in 1186 confirming the rights of the citizens of Bremen. It limited the archbishop's power over them and recognised that a serf who lived in the city for a year and a day without being…

gillo-pontecorvo.s: Gillo Pontecorvo (1919–2006) was an Italian film director and former anti-fascist partisan. His film The Battle of Algiers (1966), made in Algeria with largely non-professional actors, won the Golden Lion at Venice and became one of the most influential political films ever made.

guelma.s: Guelma is a city in north-eastern Algeria, on the site of the Roman town of Calama, whose bishop Possidius was the friend and biographer of Augustine. In May 1945, after the uprising at Sétif, it was the scene of brutal reprisals by the army and settler militias against Muslim…

generals-putsch.s: The Generals' Putsch was a failed coup in Algiers in April 1961 by four retired French generals, Maurice Challe, Edmond Jouhaud, André Zeller and Raoul Salan, who opposed Charles de Gaulle's move towards Algerian self-determination. They seized Algiers with parachute units,…

geneva-accords-1954.s: The Geneva Accords were the agreements concluded at the Geneva Conference in July 1954 that ended the First Indochina War. They provided for a ceasefire, recognised the independence of Laos and Cambodia, and temporarily divided Vietnam at the 17th parallel between the Viet…

grand-council-of-french-west-africa.n: Grand Council of French West Africa
grand-council-of-french-west-africa.s: The Grand Council of French West Africa was a federal assembly created in 1947 and sitting in Dakar, made up of councillors elected by the territorial assemblies of the federation's colonies. It voted the federal budget and gave African politicians a voice in federal affairs.

gulf-of-guinea.s: The Gulf of Guinea is the north-eastern part of the tropical Atlantic Ocean off West and Central Africa, stretching roughly from Cape Palmas in Liberia to Cape Lopez in Gabon. Its coasts include the former Gold, Slave and Ivory Coasts, and the Niger delta, and it was a centre…

german-federal-act.s: The German Federal Act of 8 June 1815 was the founding treaty of the German Confederation, agreed at the Congress of Vienna and incorporated into its Final Act. It united some thirty-nine sovereign states and free cities in a league with a permanent Federal Assembly in…

gahadavala-dynasty.s: The Gahadavala dynasty ruled a kingdom in the middle Ganges plain of northern India, centred on Varanasi and Kannauj, from the late eleventh century until the end of the twelfth. Its kings, such as Govindachandra, were patrons of Hindu temples and Brahmins.

gaero-of-baekje.s: Gaero was the twenty-first king of Baekje, reigning from 455 to 475. He sought help from the Chinese Northern Wei against Goguryeo, without success, and carried out costly building works.

gogugwon-of-goguryeo.s: Gogugwon of Goguryeo was the sixteenth king of Goguryeo, reigning from 331 to 371. In 342 the Former Yan under Murong Huang sacked his capital, carried off his mother and the body of his father King Micheon, and forced him to submit.

guanqiu-jian.s: Guanqiu Jian was a general of the Chinese state of Cao Wei during the Three Kingdoms period. In 244-245 he invaded Goguryeo, defeated King Dongcheon and sacked the capital Hwando, pursuing the king into the Okjeo country.

gyojeong-dogam.s: The Gyojeong Dogam, or Directorate General for Policy Formulation, was the office through which the Choe military house ruled the Korean kingdom of Goryeo. Created by Choe Chung-heon in 1209, it controlled appointments, taxation and the surveillance of officials, while the…

ganghwa-island.s: Ganghwa Island is an island at the mouth of the Han River on the west coast of Korea, now part of Incheon. From 1232 to 1270 it sheltered the Goryeo court from the Mongols, who could not cross its narrow straits.

goryeosa.s: The Goryeosa is the official history of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo, compiled under the Joseon dynasty by scholars including Jeong In-ji and completed in 1451. In 139 volumes it contains annals of the kings, treatises, tables and biographies.

gukjagam.s: The Gukjagam was the national Confucian academy of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo, founded in 992 by King Seongjong in the capital Kaegyong. It trained the sons of officials in the Confucian classics for the civil service.

gyeongwon-yi-clan.s: The Gyeongwon Yi clan, also known as the Incheon Yi, was one of the most powerful aristocratic lineages of the Korean kingdom of Goryeo. From the eleventh century it married daughters into the royal house and monopolised high office for about eighty years.

georg-buchner.s: Georg Büchner was a German dramatist, revolutionary and scientist, born near Darmstadt in the Grand Duchy of Hesse. In 1834 he wrote the revolutionary pamphlet Der Hessische Landbote and then fled abroad.

grand-duchess-elizabeth-feodorovna.s: Grand Duchess Elizabeth Feodorovna, born Princess Elisabeth of Hesse in Darmstadt, was a daughter of Grand Duke Louis IV and Princess Alice. In 1884 she married Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich of Russia, and after his assassination in 1905 she founded a religious community of…

gediminids.s: The Gediminids were the dynasty of grand dukes of Lithuania descended from Gediminas, who ruled from about 1316. Its members ruled Lithuania and, through the Jagiellonian branch descended from Jogaila, Poland, Bohemia and Hungary.

gaston-thorn.s: Gaston Thorn was a Luxembourg Liberal politician who served as prime minister from 1974 to 1979, leading a coalition of his Democratic Party and the Socialists. He was also President of the United Nations General Assembly in 1975–1976 and President of the European Commission…

gustav-simon.s: Gustav Simon was the Nazi Gauleiter of Koblenz-Trier, later Moselland, who headed the civil administration of occupied Luxembourg from 1940 to 1944. He pursued the Germanisation and de facto annexation of the country, banning the use of French, imposing German law and…

gilchrist-thomas-process.s: The Gilchrist–Thomas process is a method of making steel from phosphorus-rich iron ore, developed by the British cousins Sidney Gilchrist Thomas and Percy Gilchrist and made public in 1879. By lining the Bessemer converter with a basic material such as dolomite, it removed…

gian-gastone-de-medici.s: Gian Gastone de' Medici was the last Medici Grand Duke of Tuscany, reigning from 1723 to 1737. Withdrawn and often bedridden, he nonetheless relaxed his father Cosimo III's religious restrictions, reduced taxes and repealed anti-Jewish laws.

galilean-moons.s: The Galilean moons are the four largest moons of Jupiter, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, discovered by Galileo Galilei with his telescope in January 1610. He published the discovery in the Sidereus Nuncius and named them the Medicean Stars in honour of Cosimo II de' Medici…

gurjars.s: The Gurjars are a community of north-western India and Pakistan, historically pastoralists and farmers, whose name appears in sources from the sixth century CE. The Gurjara-Pratihara dynasty and the region of Gujarat take their names from them, and Arab writers called the…

gangavadi.s: Gangavadi was the region of southern Karnataka ruled by the Western Ganga dynasty from the 4th to the 10th century, with its capital eventually at Talakad on the Kaveri. The Cholas conquered it around 1004, and the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana took it from them in 1116, making…

gangaraja.s: Gangaraja was the leading general and minister of the Hoysala king Vishnuvardhana, who captured Talakad from the Cholas in 1116. A devout Jain, he restored and endowed many Jain shrines, especially at Shravanabelagola, where numerous inscriptions record his donations and his…

golkar.s: Golkar is an Indonesian political party that began in 1964 as an army-backed federation of functional groups opposed to the Communist Party. Under Suharto's New Order it served as the regime's electoral vehicle, winning every parliamentary election from 1971 to 1997 with the…

green-revolution.s: The Green Revolution was the spread of high-yielding varieties of wheat and rice, together with chemical fertilisers, pesticides and irrigation, across much of the developing world from the 1960s. Building on plant breeding in Mexico and at the International Rice Research…

guided-democracy-in-indonesia.s: Guided Democracy was the political system of Indonesia under Sukarno from 1959 to 1965. After he restored the 1945 constitution by decree in July 1959, parliament lost much of its power and Sukarno ruled by balancing the army against the Communist Party, under slogans of…

genesee-river.s: The Genesee River rises in northern Pennsylvania and flows north through western New York to Lake Ontario at Rochester. Its valley was the heartland of the Seneca, westernmost nation of the Iroquois Confederacy, whose towns there were burned by the Sullivan Expedition in 1779.

great-peace-of-montreal.s: The Great Peace of Montreal was a peace treaty signed in August 1701 by the governor of New France, Louis-Hector de Callière, and the representatives of about forty Native nations, among them the Iroquois Confederacy and France's Native allies of the Great Lakes. It ended…

gabo-reforms.s: The Gabo Reforms were a programme of reforms carried out in Korea from 1894 to 1896 by a pro-Japanese government led by Kim Hong-jip, after Japanese troops occupied the royal palace. They abolished the legal distinction between yangban and commoners, slavery, the civil service…

gapsin-coup.s: The Gapsin Coup was a failed attempt by Korean reformers led by Kim Ok-gyun to seize power in Seoul in December 1884. With the help of Japanese legation guards, they killed conservative ministers at a banquet and announced a programme of modernising reforms.

gwanghaegun-of-joseon.s: Gwanghaegun was the fifteenth king of Joseon, ruling from 1608 to 1623. As crown prince he helped lead resistance to the Japanese invasions, and as king he rebuilt the war-ravaged country, introduced the Uniform Land Tax Law in Gyeonggi province and saw the medical…

gyeongbokgung.s: Gyeongbokgung is the main royal palace of the Joseon dynasty in Seoul, built in 1395 after the capital moved to Hanyang. It was burned during the Japanese invasion of 1592 and left in ruins for more than two centuries until the regent Heungseon Daewongun rebuilt it in 1867.

gyujanggak.s: The Gyujanggak was the royal library and research institute founded by King Jeongjo in 1776 at Changdeokgung palace in Seoul. It kept the writings of former kings and a large collection of Korean and Chinese books, and its scholars, including men of illegitimate birth whom…

golden-gate-kyiv.s: The Golden Gate was the main ceremonial entrance of medieval Kyiv, built under Yaroslav the Wise around 1037 as part of the city's new fortifications, with a church above its passage. It was badly damaged when the Mongols sacked Kyiv in 1240 and later fell into ruin.

galicians.s: The Galicians are the people of Galicia, in north-western Spain, whose language, Galician, is closely related to Portuguese. In the early Middle Ages Galicia was part of the Kingdom of Asturias and later of León, and its people and nobles played a large part in the…

garcia-i-of-leon.s: García I was the eldest son of Alfonso III of Asturias and the first king of León. He rebelled against his father, who around 910 divided the realm among his sons, leaving García the lands of León, with Galicia going to Ordoño II and Asturias to Fruela II.

glyptothek.s: The Glyptothek is a museum of ancient Greek and Roman sculpture in Munich, commissioned by Ludwig I of Bavaria and built by Leo von Klenze between 1816 and 1830. It was the first public museum in Munich.

georges-lemaitre.s: Georges Lemaître was a Belgian Catholic priest, physicist and astronomer at the University of Leuven. In 1927 he proposed that the universe is expanding, deriving the relationship between distance and recession velocity of galaxies later known as Hubble's law, and in 1931…

gabunga.s: Gabunga was the title of the admiral of the Kingdom of Buganda's fleet of war canoes on Lake Victoria, a hereditary office held by the head of the Lungfish (Mamba) clan. The large plank-built canoes under his command let the kabakas raid and control the shores and islands of…

gomba.s: Gomba is a county of the Kingdom of Buganda in central Uganda, south-west of Kampala. It was absorbed by Buganda as the kingdom expanded beyond its core counties, from the seventeenth century.

geoffrey-chaucer.s: Geoffrey Chaucer was an English poet and royal official, often called the father of English literature. Working as a courtier, diplomat and customs controller in London, he wrote Troilus and Criseyde and The Canterbury Tales in the London dialect of Middle English, helping to…

gobelins-manufactory.s: The Gobelins Manufactory is a tapestry works in Paris, on the site of the dyeing workshops of the Gobelin family. In 1662 Colbert bought it for Louis XIV and made it a royal manufactory producing tapestries and furniture for the royal palaces under the painter Charles Le Brun.

george-viii-of-georgia.s: George VIII was the last king of a united Georgia, reigning from 1446. Regional lords challenged him: Bagrat of Imereti defeated him at Chikhori in 1463, and in 1465 the atabeg of Samtskhe captured him.

great-turkish-onslaught.s: The Great Turkish Onslaught, in Georgian Didi Turkoba, is the name Georgian sources give to the Seljuk Turkish invasions and settlement of Georgia from about 1080. Turkmen nomads occupied pastures, ravaged towns and farmland and drove peasants from their land, and King George…

george-brydges-rodney-1st-baron-rodney.s: George Brydges Rodney was a British naval officer best known for his victories in the American War of Independence. In 1780 he relieved Gibraltar after defeating a Spanish squadron at Cape St Vincent, and in April 1782 he defeated the French fleet of the Comte de Grasse at the…

georgios-papandreou.s: George Papandreou was a Greek liberal politician who led the government in exile and returned to liberated Athens in 1944. He founded the Centre Union party, which won the elections of 1963 and 1964, and as Prime Minister he clashed with the young King Constantine II over…

george-seferis.s: George Seferis, born Giorgos Seferiadis near Smyrna, was a Greek poet and diplomat. His collections, beginning with Strophe in 1931, combined modernist technique with Greek history and myth and the experience of the lost Greek world of Asia Minor.

georgios-papadopoulos.s: Georgios Papadopoulos was a Greek army colonel who led the military coup of 21 April 1967 and headed the junta that ruled Greece until 1974. After the king's failed counter-coup of December 1967 he made himself Prime Minister, and later also regent.

grammos.s: Grammos is a mountain range on the border between north-western Greece and Albania, rising to about 2,520 metres. During the Greek Civil War it was the main stronghold of the communist Democratic Army, and in August 1949 the government army under Alexandros Papagos took it,…

georgios-kondylis.s: Georgios Kondylis was a Greek army officer and politician, at first a supporter of Eleftherios Venizelos. He took part in several coups and briefly led a government in 1926.

greek-civil-war.s: The Greek Civil War was fought from 1946 to 1949 between the government army, supported by Britain and then the United States, and the communist-led Democratic Army of Greece. It grew out of conflict between the resistance movement EAM-ELAS and the returning government in 1944.

gerard-of-csanad.s: Gerard of Csanád was a Venetian-born Benedictine monk who became tutor to Stephen I's son Emeric and, around 1030, the first bishop of Csanád (Cenad) in southern Hungary. He was killed in Buda during the pagan uprising of 1046, according to legend thrown from the hill now…

geza-ii-of-hungary.s: Géza II was king of Hungary from 1141 to 1162. He defended the kingdom against German and Byzantine pressure, intervened repeatedly in the wars of Kievan Rus', and invited German settlers, later known as the Transylvanian Saxons, to southern Transylvania.

greater-caucasus.s: The Greater Caucasus is the main range of the Caucasus Mountains, running about 1,200 kilometres from the Black Sea to the Caspian and rising to 5,642 metres at Mount Elbrus. Its passes, especially the Darial Pass, and the coastal route at Derbent were the gateways through…

gurgenes.s: Gurgenes was a king of Iberia in eastern Georgia in the 520s, known from the Byzantine historian Procopius. When the Persian king Kavad I tried to impose Persian burial customs, Gurgenes rebelled and appealed to Emperor Justin I, but no effective help came, and when a Persian…

gottlob-curt-heinrich-von-tottleben.s: Gottlob Curt Heinrich von Tottleben was a Saxon-born general in Russian service. During the Seven Years' War he occupied Berlin in 1760 but was later convicted of secret dealings with the Prussians.

george-berkeley.s: George Berkeley was an Irish philosopher and Anglican bishop of Cloyne, educated at Trinity College Dublin. In works such as A Treatise Concerning the Principles of Human Knowledge (1710) he argued for immaterialism, the view that physical objects exist only as perceived.

gilead.s: Gilead is the hilly region east of the Jordan River, on both sides of the Jabbok, in present-day north-western Jordan. Israelite tribes settled there, and it was long contested between the Kingdom of Israel and Aram-Damascus until Tiglath-pileser III annexed it to Assyria…

giacomo-matteotti.s: Giacomo Matteotti was an Italian socialist politician, secretary of the Unitary Socialist Party. In May 1924 he denounced violence and fraud in the elections in a speech to the Chamber of Deputies; on 10 June he was kidnapped and murdered in Rome by Fascist squad members.

giacomo-puccini.s: Giacomo Puccini was an Italian composer, the leading figure of Italian opera after Giuseppe Verdi. His works, including La bohème (1896), Tosca (1900), Madama Butterfly (1904) and the unfinished Turandot, combine lyrical melody with realistic drama and remain among the most…

guglielmo-marconi.s: Guglielmo Marconi was an Italian inventor and engineer who developed practical long-distance radio telegraphy. He patented his system in Britain in 1896 and in 1901 received the first transatlantic radio signal, sent from Cornwall to Newfoundland.

gedaliah.s: Gedaliah son of Ahikam was a Judahite official whom the Babylonians appointed governor of Judah after the destruction of Jerusalem in 587 or 586 BCE. He governed from Mizpah and urged the survivors to serve Babylon, but within months he was assassinated by Ishmael son of…

george-harris-1st-baron-harris.s: George Harris, 1st Baron Harris (1746–1829), was a British army officer who served in the American War of Independence, where he was wounded at Bunker Hill. As commander-in-chief of the Madras army he led the British and Hyderabadi forces that invaded Mysore in the Fourth…

giambattista-vico.s: Giambattista Vico (1668–1744) was a Neapolitan philosopher and professor of rhetoric at the University of Naples. In his New Science (1725) he argued that human societies pass through recurring ages of gods, heroes and men, and that history can be understood because people…

giovanni-pontano.s: Giovanni Pontano (1426–1503) was an Italian humanist, poet and statesman. Born in Umbria, he served the Aragonese kings of Naples for decades as secretary and chief minister under Ferrante.

garcia-sanchez-iii-of-pamplona.s: García Sánchez III (c. 1012–1054) was king of Pamplona from 1035, the eldest legitimate son of Sancho III the Great.

gebhard-leberecht-von-blucher.s: Gebhard Leberecht von Blücher (1742–1819) was a Prussian field marshal of the Napoleonic Wars. Known as Marshal Forwards, he won the Battle of the Katzbach and fought at Leipzig in 1813, then led his army across the Rhine into France.

german-cruiser-blucher.s: Blücher was an Admiral Hipper-class heavy cruiser of the German navy, commissioned in 1939. On 9 April 1940, leading the force sent to seize Oslo during the invasion of Norway, she was sunk in the Drøbak Narrows by guns and torpedoes from the old Oscarsborg fortress.

giresun.s: Giresun, the ancient Kerasous (Cerasus), is a port city on the Black Sea coast of north-eastern Turkey. Founded as a Greek colony of Sinope, it came under the kings of Pontus in the second century BCE and later belonged to the Roman and Byzantine empires and the Empire of…

gaius-valerius-triarius.s: Gaius Valerius Triarius was a Roman legate under Lucullus in the Third Mithridatic War. In 67 BCE, while Lucullus was away, he attacked Mithridates VI near Zela in Pontus and suffered a heavy defeat in which, according to ancient writers, thousands of Romans and many officers…

germanus-of-auxerre.s: Germanus of Auxerre was a Gallo-Roman bishop of Auxerre who visited Britain in 429, and perhaps again later, to oppose the Pelagian heresy. His Life records that he led the Britons to a bloodless 'Alleluia victory' over Picts and Saxons.

glyndyfrdwy.s: Glyndyfrdwy is a village and former lordship in the Dee valley of north-east Wales, between Corwen and Llangollen. It was held by descendants of the princes of northern Powys, among them Owain Glyndŵr, who took his name from it.

general-state-laws-for-the-prussian-stat.n: General State Laws for the Prussian States
general-state-laws-for-the-prussian-stat.s: The General State Laws for the Prussian States (Allgemeines Landrecht) was the great Prussian law code that came into force in 1794. Begun on Frederick II's orders and drafted by Carl Gottlieb Svarez and others, it set out in about 19,000 paragraphs civil, criminal,…

georg-wilhelm-friedrich-hegel.s: Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel was a German philosopher, the leading figure of German idealism after Kant. His works, including the Phenomenology of Spirit (1807) and the Elements of the Philosophy of Right (1820), present history as the development of reason and freedom.

gustav-adolf-von-gotzen.s: Gustav Adolf von Götzen was a German officer and explorer. In 1894 he led the first European expedition to cross Rwanda, meeting King Kigeli IV Rwabugiri and reaching Lake Kivu.

giovanni-battista-bogino.s: Giovanni Battista Lorenzo Bogino was a Piedmontese statesman and minister of Charles Emmanuel III of Sardinia, responsible for war and for the affairs of Sardinia from 1759 to 1773. He pursued reforms on the island, refounding the universities of Cagliari and Sassari in the…

gavin-douglas.s: Gavin Douglas was a Scottish poet and bishop of Dunkeld, a son of the Earl of Angus. His Eneados, a translation of Virgil's Aeneid into Scots verse completed in 1513, was the first complete translation of a major classical poem into any form of English.

george-of-antioch.s: George of Antioch was a Greek Christian who served the Zirid rulers of Mahdia before becoming the leading minister and admiral of Roger II of Sicily, with the title emir of emirs. His fleets captured Tripoli in 1146 and Mahdia in 1148, creating a short-lived Sicilian dominion…

giacomo-da-lentini.s: Giacomo da Lentini was a notary at the court of the emperor Frederick II and the leading poet of the Sicilian School, which wrote love lyrics in a refined Sicilian vernacular. He is usually credited with inventing the sonnet.

giuseppe-verdi.s: Giuseppe Verdi was an Italian opera composer, born at Le Roncole near Busseto in the Duchy of Parma. His operas, among them Nabucco, Rigoletto, La traviata, Il trovatore, Aida, Otello and Falstaff, made him the dominant figure of nineteenth-century Italian opera.

glastonbury-abbey.s: Glastonbury Abbey was a Benedictine monastery in Somerset, south-west England, founded by the seventh century and patronised by the West Saxon kings. Reformed by Dunstan in the tenth century, it became one of the richest abbeys in England and was linked in legend with Joseph…

godwin-earl-of-wessex.s: Godwin was an Anglo-Saxon nobleman who rose under Cnut to become Earl of Wessex and the most powerful man in England after the king. His daughter Edith married Edward the Confessor, but a quarrel with the king led to the exile of Godwin's family in 1051 until their armed…

goppingen.s: Göppingen is a town in Baden-Württemberg, Germany, on the River Fils east of Stuttgart. Lying below the Hohenstaufen hill, the ancestral seat of the Staufer emperors, it became an industrial town in the nineteenth century, and the toy and model railway maker Märklin, founded…

government-museum-mathura.s: The Government Museum, Mathura, in Uttar Pradesh, India, was founded in 1874 and holds one of the finest collections of early Indian sculpture. Its galleries are rich in Kushan and Gupta works of the Mathura school, including early images of the Buddha and the headless statue…

giovanni-maria-leria.s: Giovanni Maria Leria was an Italian Jesuit missionary who lived in Vientiane, capital of Lan Xang, in the 1640s during the reign of Sourigna Vongsa. He made few converts, but his account of the kingdom, published by the Jesuit Giovanni Filippo de Marini, is one of the earliest…

gianh-river.s: The Gianh River is a river of Quảng Bình Province in central Vietnam. From the 17th century it marked the frontier between the territory of the Trịnh lords in the north and the Nguyễn lords in the south, a division that lasted from the truce of 1672 until the Tây Sơn wars of…

gang-gam-chan.s: Gang Gam-chan was a Korean scholar-official and general of the Goryeo dynasty. As commander against the third Khitan invasion, he destroyed the Liao army at the Battle of Gwiju in 1019, a victory that secured Goryeo's independence.

george-weah.s: George Weah is a Liberian footballer and politician. A striker for clubs including Monaco, Paris Saint-Germain and AC Milan, he was named FIFA World Player of the Year and won the Ballon d'Or in 1995, the first African to do so.

gaius-julius-lacer.s: Gaius Julius Lacer was a Roman architect of the early 2nd century CE, known as the builder of the Alcántara Bridge over the Tagus in Lusitania, completed under Trajan around 104–106. An inscription in the small temple at the end of the bridge names him as its builder and…

george-william-elector-of-brandenburg.s: George William was Elector of Brandenburg and Duke of Prussia from 1619 to 1640. Weak and indecisive, he tried to stay out of the Thirty Years' War but could not keep Swedish or imperial armies out of his lands, which were devastated.

gutsherrschaft.s: Gutsherrschaft is the German term for the manorial system that developed east of the Elbe from the 15th and 16th centuries. Noble landlords, such as the Junkers of Brandenburg and Prussia, ran large grain-producing estates worked by peasants bound to them by heavy labour…

general-war-commissariat.s: The General War Commissariat (Generalkriegskommissariat) was a central authority of Brandenburg-Prussia that grew up under the Great Elector to supply and finance the standing army. Levying taxes across the Hohenzollern lands from Cleves to Prussia, it became the main…

gregor-mendel.s: Gregor Mendel was an Augustinian friar and scientist from Austrian Silesia who became abbot of St Thomas's Abbey in Brno, Moravia. Through experiments on pea plants in the monastery garden between 1856 and 1863 he discovered the basic laws of heredity, published in 1866.

gilukhipa.s: Gilukhipa was a Mitanni princess, daughter of King Shuttarna II, who was sent to Egypt to marry Pharaoh Amenhotep III in his tenth regnal year, around 1380 BCE. A commemorative scarab records her arrival with 317 women of her household.

giovanni-battista-cairato.s: Giovanni Battista Cairato was an Italian military architect from Milan who served Philip II as chief engineer of the Portuguese possessions in Asia from the 1580s. He designed or rebuilt fortifications across the Estado da Índia, the Portuguese state in India, including Fort…

goncalo-da-silveira.s: Gonçalo da Silveira was a Portuguese Jesuit missionary who in 1560–1561 travelled to the court of the Mwene Mutapa in present-day Zimbabwe and baptised the king and members of his family. Muslim traders at the court persuaded the king that the missionary was a spy and…

gatsi-rusere.s: Gatsi Rusere was a ruler of the Mutapa kingdom from about 1589 to 1623. Faced with rebellions and invasions, he relied more and more on Portuguese military help, and in 1607 he signed a treaty ceding to Portugal the gold, copper, iron, lead and tin mines of his kingdom in…

gauleiter.s: A Gauleiter was the Nazi Party's leader of a regional branch, or Gau, in Germany and later in annexed territories. Appointed by Hitler and answerable to him alone, Gauleiters often also held state offices such as Reich governor, and during the Second World War, as Reich…

genocide-convention.s: The Genocide Convention, formally the Convention on the Prevention and Punishment of the Crime of Genocide, was adopted by the United Nations General Assembly on 9 December 1948 and came into force in 1951. Drawing on the work of the lawyer Raphael Lemkin and the experience of…

german-labour-front.s: The German Labour Front was the Nazi organisation that replaced the trade unions after they were dissolved in May 1933. Led by Robert Ley, it enrolled employers and workers together, reaching more than 20 million members, and controlled wages, workplace discipline and leisure…

gulf-of-mexico.s: The Gulf of Mexico is an arm of the Atlantic Ocean bordered by the United States, Mexico and Cuba. The Mississippi and other great rivers drain into it, and explorers such as La Salle, who reached the Mississippi's mouth in 1682, used it to claim the interior of North America.

greenpeace.s: Greenpeace is an international environmental organisation that grew out of a 1971 protest voyage from Vancouver against American nuclear tests in Alaska. It became known for direct action at sea against nuclear testing, whaling and pollution.

gia-dinh.s: Gia Định was the name of the Vietnamese settlement and citadel on the site of present-day Ho Chi Minh City, and of the surrounding province of southern Vietnam. Nguyen Anh took it from the Tây Sơn in 1788 and made it his base for the reconquest of the country.

gia-long-code.s: The Gia Long Code, officially Hoàng Việt luật lệ, was the legal code of the Nguyen dynasty, promulgated by Emperor Gia Long in 1815. Closely modelled on the code of the Qing dynasty, it replaced the Lê code and organised criminal, administrative and family law in about four…

gulf-of-finland.s: The Gulf of Finland is the easternmost arm of the Baltic Sea, lying between Finland to the north and Estonia to the south, with St Petersburg at its eastern end. In the Middle Ages it carried the trade between the Hanseatic towns and Novgorod via the Neva, and Reval (Tallinn)…

gaius-laelius.s: Gaius Laelius was a Roman general and statesman, the close friend and lieutenant of Publius Cornelius Scipio Africanus in the Second Punic War. He commanded the fleet at the capture of New Carthage in 209 BCE, helped Masinissa defeat and capture Syphax in 203 BCE and led the…

gulussa.s: Gulussa was a Numidian prince, a son of King Masinissa. On his father's death in 148 BCE, Scipio Aemilianus divided the royal functions among the three legitimate sons, and Gulussa received command of the army, which he led on the Roman side in the Third Punic War.

gulf-of-gabes.s: The Gulf of Gabès, known in antiquity as the Lesser Syrtis, is a gulf of the Mediterranean on the eastern coast of Tunisia, between Sfax and the island of Djerba. Its shallows and shifting sandbanks made it notorious among ancient sailors.

gaius-scribonius-curio-tribune-50-bce.s: Gaius Scribonius Curio was a Roman politician who, as tribune of the plebs in 50 BCE, defended Julius Caesar's interests in the Senate in the months before the civil war. At its outbreak Caesar sent him to secure Sicily and then Africa.

gaius-poppaeus-sabinus.s: Gaius Poppaeus Sabinus was a Roman senator, consul in 9 CE, who governed Moesia for about twenty-four years under Augustus and Tiberius, also holding Macedonia and Achaea. In 26 CE he crushed a revolt of Thracian mountain tribes against conscription into the Roman army, as…

golyama-kosmatka.s: Golyama Kosmatka is a Thracian burial mound near Shipka in the Kazanlak Valley of Bulgaria. Excavated in 2004 by Georgi Kitov, it contains a monumental stone tomb thought to be that of the Odrysian king Seuthes III.

george-russell-clerk.s: Sir George Russell Clerk was a British administrator who spent most of his career in India, twice serving as governor of Bombay. In 1853–1854 he was special commissioner for the Orange River Sovereignty, sent to end British rule there, and on 23 February 1854 he signed the…

grey-college-bloemfontein.s: Grey College is a boys' school in Bloemfontein, South Africa, founded in 1855 and named after Sir George Grey, governor of the Cape Colony, who supported its establishment. One of the oldest schools in the former Orange Free State, it gave rise in 1904 to Grey University…

gawdawpalin-temple.s: The Gawdawpalin Temple is one of the largest temples of Pagan (Bagan) in central Myanmar. Begun under King Narapatisithu and completed under his son Htilominlo in the early thirteenth century, it is a two-storeyed brick temple with stucco decoration, among the last great…

grantha-script.s: The Grantha script is a South Indian script derived from Brahmi, used from Pallava times to write Sanskrit in the Tamil country, where the Tamil script lacked letters for many Sanskrit sounds. It was used for Sanskrit texts and inscriptions until the twentieth century, is the…

gian-lorenzo-bernini.s: Gian Lorenzo Bernini was an Italian sculptor and architect, the leading artist of Baroque Rome. Working for successive popes, he designed the bronze baldacchino and the great colonnade of St Peter's Square at the Vatican, the Fountain of the Four Rivers in Piazza Navona, and…

gang-of-four.s: The Gang of Four was the radical faction of the Chinese Communist Party that rose to power during the Cultural Revolution: Mao Zedong's wife Jiang Qing, Zhang Chunqiao, Yao Wenyuan and Wang Hongwen. They were arrested on 6 October 1976, a month after Mao's death, blamed for…

grignoux.s: The Grignoux were the popular, anti-princely faction in the city of Liège in the first half of the seventeenth century, opposed by the Chiroux, who supported the prince-bishop. Their struggle over the city's liberties ended when Prince-Bishop Ferdinand of Bavaria took the city…

glarentza.s: Glarentza was a medieval port on the north-western coast of the Peloponnese, near modern Kyllini, and the main harbour of the Principality of Achaea, where its mint struck coins. It passed to Constantine Palaiologos in 1428 and was later largely abandoned.

generalitat-de-catalunya.s: The Generalitat de Catalunya began as the Diputació del General, a standing committee created by the Corts of Cervera in 1359 to collect the taxes voted by the Catalan Courts. It became the chief defender of the Principality's constitutions, was abolished in 1716, and was…

ginevra-de-benci.s: Ginevra de' Benci is a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a young Florentine noblewoman, painted around 1474–1478. Long in the collection of the princes of Liechtenstein, it was sold in 1967 to the National Gallery of Art in Washington, the only painting by Leonardo in the…

grigore-ureche.s: Grigore Ureche was a Moldavian boyar and chronicler who wrote the first chronicle of Moldavia in Romanian, covering 1359 to 1594. He argued for the Latin origin of the Romanian language and people.

golestan-palace.s: The Golestan Palace is a royal complex in central Tehran, developed from a Safavid citadel into the chief residence of the Qajar shahs after Tehran became the capital in the late eighteenth century. Rebuilt and decorated in the nineteenth century, it blends Persian and…

ganitasarasangraha.s: The Ganitasarasangraha is a Sanskrit treatise on mathematics written about 850 by the Jain mathematician Mahaviracharya at the Rashtrakuta court of Amoghavarsha I. It covers arithmetic, fractions, geometry, the rules of zero, quadratic equations and permutations and…

govinda-ii.s: Govinda II was Rashtrakuta emperor of the Deccan from about 774 to 780, the son and successor of Krishna I. His short reign, in which he is said to have neglected government, was ended by his younger brother Dhruva Dharavarsha, who defeated him and his allies in a struggle for…

govinda-iv.s: Govinda IV was Rashtrakuta emperor of the Deccan from about 930 to 936, a son of Indra III who took the throne from his elder brother Amoghavarsha II. His reign was remembered for misgovernment and dissolute conduct.

gunabhadra.s: Gunabhadra was a Digambara Jain monk and author of the ninth century, a disciple of Jinasena, working in the Rashtrakuta empire. He completed his teacher's unfinished Adipurana and wrote the Uttarapurana, which together form the Mahapurana, the Sanskrit history of the 63…

german-busch.s: Germán Busch was a Bolivian army officer, a hero of the Chaco War, who became president in 1937 after overthrowing David Toro. Continuing 'military socialism', he issued a labour code, convened a convention that wrote the social constitution of 1938 and in 1939 ordered mining…

gonzalo-sanchez-de-lozada.s: Gonzalo Sánchez de Lozada was president of Bolivia from 1993 to 1997 and from 2002 to 2003. As planning minister in 1985 he designed the New Economic Policy that ended hyperinflation.

gabriela-mistral.s: Gabriela Mistral, born Lucila Godoy Alcayaga, was a Chilean poet, educator and diplomat. In 1945 she became the first Latin American writer to win the Nobel Prize in Literature.

galo-plaza.s: Galo Plaza Lasso was president of Ecuador from 1948 to 1952, the first in decades to complete a full term. His government encouraged the banana boom that made Ecuador the world's largest banana exporter and respected civil liberties.

guillermo-lasso.s: Guillermo Lasso is an Ecuadorian banker and centre-right politician who was president from 2021 to 2023. His government ran a rapid COVID-19 vaccination campaign but faced mass protests, prison massacres and rising crime.

gerardo-barrios.s: Gerardo Barrios was a Salvadoran general and liberal president from 1859 to 1863, a follower of Francisco Morazán's dream of Central American union. He promoted coffee cultivation, education and a professional army, and clashed with the Church.

giano-della-bella.s: Giano della Bella (died c. 1306) was a Florentine nobleman who became a leader of the popular party against the magnates.

giovanni-boccaccio.s: Giovanni Boccaccio (1313–1375) was an Italian writer and humanist, born in or near Florence, who spent his youth in Naples in the circle of the court of King Robert of Anjou. His Decameron, a collection of a hundred tales told by young Florentines escaping the Black Death of…

girolamo-savonarola.s: Girolamo Savonarola (1452–1498) was a Dominican friar from Ferrara who preached in Florence from 1490, denouncing corruption in the church and the luxury of the Medici. After the expulsion of the Medici in 1494 he dominated the restored republic, promoting moral reform and the…

giuliano-de-medici.s: Giuliano de' Medici (1453–1478) was the younger brother of Lorenzo de' Medici and a prominent figure of Florentine society, celebrated in the poetry of Poliziano. On 26 April 1478 he was stabbed to death in Florence Cathedral by members of the Pazzi conspiracy, who also…

gonfaloniere-of-justice.s: The Gonfaloniere of Justice was the highest office of the Republic of Florence, created by the Ordinances of Justice of 1293 to command a militia enforcing the laws against the magnates. The Gonfaloniere headed the Signoria with the priors, serving like them for two months at…

giovanni-giustiniani-longo.s: Giovanni Giustiniani Longo (died 1453) was a Genoese soldier from a leading family of Chios who brought some 700 men to Constantinople in January 1453. Emperor Constantine XI placed him in command of the defence of the land walls during the Ottoman siege.

giovanni-scriba.s: Giovanni Scriba was a Genoese notary of the twelfth century whose surviving register, covering the years 1154 to 1164, is the oldest notarial cartulary in Europe. Its more than a thousand contracts record the commenda partnerships, loans, sales and marriage agreements of…

guglielmo-boccanegra.s: Guglielmo Boccanegra (died 1274) was a Genoese merchant leader who became the first Captain of the People of Genoa in 1257 after a popular revolt against the nobility. He negotiated the Treaty of Nymphaeum with the Byzantine emperor Michael VIII Palaiologos in 1261, but his…

guatemalan-national-revolutionary-unity.s: The Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unity (URNG) was a coalition of four leftist guerrilla organisations formed in 1982 to fight the military governments in the civil war. After years of negotiations mediated by the United Nations it signed the final peace agreement with the…

gustavo-alvarez-martinez.s: Gustavo Álvarez Martínez (1937–1989) was a Honduran general who commanded the armed forces from 1982 to 1984 and was the most powerful figure in the country during the early years of US-backed operations against Sandinista Nicaragua. Trained in Argentina, he oversaw a campaign…

guntis-ulmanis.s: Guntis Ulmanis is a Latvian politician who was president of Latvia from 1993 to 1999, the first head of state after the restoration of independence. Elected by the fifth Saeima in July 1993, he oversaw the withdrawal of Russian troops in 1994 and Latvia's first steps towards…

gitanas-nauseda.s: Gitanas Nausėda is a Lithuanian economist and politician who has been president of Lithuania since 2019. A former bank economist without party affiliation, he won the 2019 election against Ingrida Šimonytė and was re-elected in 2024.

guillermo-endara.s: Guillermo Endara was a Panamanian lawyer and politician who won the presidential election of May 1989 as the opposition candidate, only for Manuel Noriega to annul the result. He was sworn in on a US military base as American forces invaded in December 1989 and served as…

gatun-lake.s: Gatun Lake is an artificial lake in Panama formed by the Gatun Dam on the Chagres River, built between 1907 and 1913, and on completion the largest man-made lake in the world. It forms a major part of the Panama Canal route, carrying ships 26 metres above sea level between the…

guna-yala.s: Guna Yala, formerly San Blas, is an indigenous territory (comarca) of the Guna people along Panama's north-eastern Caribbean coast, including some 365 islands. After the Guna Revolution of 1925 against attempts to suppress their customs, the Guna gained autonomy, recognised in…

grace-contract.s: The Grace Contract was an agreement signed in 1888 and ratified in 1889 between the Peruvian government and its British bondholders, negotiated by Michael Grace. Peru's foreign debt was cancelled in exchange for control of the state railways for 66 years, guano shipments,…

gustavo-gutierrez.s: Gustavo Gutiérrez was a Peruvian Catholic priest and theologian, regarded as the founder of liberation theology. His book A Theology of Liberation, published in Spanish in 1971, argued that the church must stand with the poor and confront social injustice.

giorgione.s: Giorgione was a Venetian painter of the High Renaissance from Castelfranco Veneto. Very few works are securely attributed to him, among them The Tempest and the Castelfranco altarpiece, but his poetic landscapes, soft modelling and enigmatic subjects transformed Venetian…

giovanni-bellini.s: Giovanni Bellini was a Venetian painter who, more than anyone, made Venice a leading centre of Renaissance art. His altarpieces, such as the San Zaccaria Altarpiece, and his many Madonnas used oil paint, rich colour and natural light in new ways.

general-peoples-congress.s: The General People's Congress is a Yemeni political party founded in 1982 by President Ali Abdullah Saleh in North Yemen. After unification in 1990 it remained the ruling party, winning every parliamentary election until 2011, and served as the main vehicle of Saleh's patronage.

gaius-cassius-longinus.s: Gaius Cassius Longinus was a Roman senator and general, one of the leaders of the conspiracy that assassinated Julius Caesar in 44 BCE. Gathering forces in the East, he defeated the Rhodian fleet in 43 or 42 BCE and sacked the city of Rhodes for refusing to support him.

geoffrey-of-monmouth.s: Geoffrey of Monmouth was a Welsh-born cleric and writer whose History of the Kings of Britain (c. 1136) presented a largely legendary history of Britain from the Trojan Brutus to the seventh century.

gaius-cornelius-gallus.s: Gaius Cornelius Gallus was a Roman poet and soldier who became the first prefect of Egypt after its annexation in 30 BCE. He suppressed a revolt in the Thebaid and campaigned to the First Cataract, recording his deeds in a boastful trilingual inscription at Philae.

gaius-petronius-prefect-of-egypt.s: Gaius Petronius was Roman prefect of Egypt in the 20s BCE. After the Kushites raided the south and carried off statues of Augustus, he marched up the Nile, defeated the Kushite army and sacked Napata in about 24 BCE.

gosamaru.s: Gosamaru was a Ryukyuan lord and military commander of the fifteenth century, known for building the castle of Zakimi and strengthening Nakagusuku. In 1458 his rival Amawari, lord of Katsuren, accused him of plotting rebellion; royal forces attacked Nakagusuku and Gosamaru…

gusuku-sites-and-related-properties-of-t.n: Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu
gusuku-sites-and-related-properties-of-t.s: The Gusuku Sites and Related Properties of the Kingdom of Ryukyu are a group of nine sites on Okinawa inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000. They include the castles of Shuri, Nakijin, Zakimi, Katsuren and Nakagusuku, the royal mausoleum of Tamaudun, the…

gautami-balashri.s: Gautami Balashri was a Satavahana queen, mother of Gautamiputra Satakarni. Her Nashik cave inscription, made in the reign of her grandson Vasishthiputra Pulumavi, praises her son as a destroyer of the Shakas, Yavanas and Pahlavas and an upholder of the four varnas, and records…

gatha-saptashati.s: The Gatha Saptashati, 'Seven Hundred Verses', is an anthology of short poems in Maharashtri Prakrit attributed to the Satavahana king Hala. Its two-line verses, many spoken by women, deal with love, separation and village life.

gregory-tsamblak.s: Gregory Tsamblak was a Bulgarian churchman and writer of the Tarnovo literary school. After the Ottoman conquest he worked in Serbia and Moldavia, and in 1415 he became metropolitan of Kiev under Lithuanian protection, attending the Council of Constance in 1418.

george-i-terter.s: George I Terter was tsar of Bulgaria from 1280 to 1292 and founder of the Terter dynasty, a noble family of Cuman origin. His reign was dominated by the Golden Horde warlord Nogai, to whom he had to submit and send his son Theodore Svetoslav as a hostage.
